items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8)** Sommerville divides *development testing* into which three activities?
options: Unit testing, component testing, system testing
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8: development testing (by the team developing the system) = unit testing (individual units/objects), component testing (composite components/interfaces), and system testing (the integrated system).

items.q: **(Pressman — basis path testing / McCabe)** Cyclomatic complexity gives which of the following?
options: The exact runtime of the program
The number of independent paths — an upper bound on the tests needed to cover every statement and branch
The number of lines of code
items.explain: Pressman (McCabe): cyclomatic complexity = the number of linearly independent paths through a program, giving an upper bound on the number of tests required to guarantee every statement and branch is executed.

items.q: **(Pressman)** For a control flow graph, cyclomatic complexity V(G) can be computed as all of these EXCEPT:
options: Number of regions of the planar graph
items.explain: Pressman gives three equivalent computations: V(G) = E − N + 2; V(G) = (predicate nodes) + 1; V(G) = number of regions. It has nothing to do with LOC/10.

items.q: **(Pressman — black-box testing)** Equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis are examples of:
options: Black-box testing — deriving tests from the specification, not the code
items.explain: Pressman: equivalence partitioning (divide input into classes) and BVA (test at the edges) are black-box techniques derived from the specification/requirements, with no knowledge of internal code structure.

items.q: **(Pressman — unit testing)** In unit testing, a module that simulates a *lower-level* module CALLED by the unit under test is a:
items.explain: Pressman: a stub replaces a subordinate (called) module; a driver replaces a superordinate (calling) module. Stubs are used in top-down integration, drivers in bottom-up.

items.q: **(Pressman — integration testing)** Integrating modules from the top of the control hierarchy downward, using stubs for not-yet-integrated modules, is:
items.explain: Pressman: top-down integration moves from the main control module downward (depth- or breadth-first), replacing subordinate modules with stubs. Bottom-up starts at the leaves using drivers.

items.q: **(Pressman/Sommerville)** Alpha testing differs from beta testing in that alpha testing is conducted:
options: By end users at their own site, uncontrolled
At the developer's site by end users in a controlled environment
items.explain: Alpha testing is performed at the developer's site by end users with the developer observing, in a controlled setting. Beta testing happens at end-user sites, 'live', without the developer present.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8 — V&V)** The distinction between verification and validation is:
options: Verification: are we building the product right (to spec)? Validation: are we building the right product (to user needs)?
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8 (Boehm): verification checks conformance to specification ('building the product right'); validation checks that the product meets the customer's real needs ('building the right product').

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8 — testing goals)** Sommerville distinguishes two goals of software testing. They are:
options: Validation testing (show it meets requirements) and defect testing (find incorrect behaviour)
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8: the two goals are validation testing (demonstrate the software meets its requirements) and defect testing (find inputs where behaviour is incorrect/undesirable).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8 — release testing)** Release testing is primarily a form of ___ testing whose goal is to ___:
options: black-box; convince the supplier the system is good enough to release (not to find defects)
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8: release testing is black-box (specification-based) testing of a release by a team separate from developers, aiming to demonstrate the system is good enough for use — a Go/No-Go decision, not primarily defect hunting.

items.q: **(Sommerville/Pressman — stress testing)** Designing tests that deliberately exceed the system's design limits is:
items.explain: Stress testing pushes the system beyond its specified loads/limits to find failure behaviour and check graceful degradation, exposing defects that only appear under overload.

items.q: **(Pressman — SCM)** A baseline in software configuration management is best defined as:
options: A specification or product reviewed and agreed upon, that thereafter changes only through formal change control
items.explain: Pressman/IEEE: a baseline is a specification or product formally reviewed and agreed upon, serving as a basis for further development; it can be changed only through formal change-control procedures.

items.q: **(Pressman — change control)** In Pressman's change-control process, an approved change is formally authorized by issuing an:
items.explain: Pressman: after a change request is evaluated and the Change Control Authority (CCA/CCB) approves it, an Engineering Change Order (ECO) is generated describing the change, constraints, and review criteria.

items.q: **(Pressman — SCM process)** Which is one of the core tasks of the SCM process?
options: Version control, change control, and configuration auditing
items.explain: Pressman: the SCM process comprises identification, version control, change control, configuration auditing, and reporting — managing change to Software Configuration Items (SCIs).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch25 — version management)** In version management terminology, a 'codeline' is:
options: A single line of source code
A sequence of versions of a component, with later versions derived from earlier ones
items.explain: Sommerville Ch25: a codeline is a sequence of versions of source code, with later versions derived from earlier ones; a baseline is a definition of a specific system (a collection of component versions).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch25 — system building)** System building is the process of:
options: Compiling and linking components into an executable system
items.explain: Sommerville Ch25: system building creates an executable system by compiling and linking the appropriate versions of components and libraries — ideally automated and reproducible (CI).

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch15 / Fagan — inspections)** Software inspections are a form of ___ that ___:
options: static verification; examines the source representation without executing it
items.explain: Inspections are static verification — people examine the static representation (code/design) to find defects without execution. Studies show high detection rates (e.g. Fagan inspections), and they don't require a runnable system.

items.q: **(Sommerville — TDD/automation)** Regression testing is most practical when:
options: Automated, so the full test set can be re-run cheaply after every change
items.explain: Sommerville: regression testing checks that changes haven't broken existing functionality; it's only economically feasible when automated, so the whole suite re-runs quickly after each change (a core CI practice).

items.q: **(Sommerville — DevOps)** A central principle of DevOps is:
options: Strictly separate development and operations teams
The same team that develops a system is responsible for deploying and supporting it, with heavy automation
items.explain: Sommerville's DevOps principles: integrate development and operations into one team responsible for the whole lifecycle, automate everything possible (CI/CD), and measure/monitor in production — enabling frequent, reliable releases.

items.q: **(Pressman/Sommerville — secure & defensive coding)** Validating all input from untrusted sources and applying least privilege are examples of:
items.explain: Validating untrusted input, default-deny access, least privilege, heeding compiler warnings, and sanitizing data to subsystems are secure/defensive programming practices that prevent vulnerabilities like injection and buffer overflows.
